title: Edema: why fluid causes swelling and when to get help
intro: Edema means swelling caused by fluid collecting in body tissues. Shoes or rings may feel tight, an arm or leg may feel heavy, or the skin may look stretched. Some swelling follows prolonged sitting or standing, but new or persistent swelling can also signal illness. The location, speed of onset and accompanying symptoms help determine how urgently it should be assessed; appearance alone does not establish the cause.

sections.heading: Different patterns provide clues, not a diagnosis
paragraphs: Swelling may affect a single limb, both legs, the face or more widespread areas. Sometimes pressing the skin leaves a dent, called pitting; other swelling does not pit. Neither finding identifies the cause by itself. Note whether swelling began suddenly, changes through the day, follows an injury or comes with pain, warmth, redness, breathlessness or reduced urine. Fluid can also collect in the lungs or abdomen, so not all important fluid retention is visible at the ankles.

sections.heading: Possible causes include circulation and organ problems
paragraphs: Veins that do not return blood effectively can contribute to leg swelling. A blood clot, infection or inflammation may cause more local swelling. Lymphatic drainage problems can produce lymphoedema, including after some cancer treatments. Heart, kidney or liver disease and low blood protein can cause fluid retention. Medicines can also contribute. Mild swelling may occur with heat, immobility or pregnancy, but those explanations should not be assumed for a new concerning change. More than one cause can be present.

sections.heading: Recognise urgent warning signs
paragraphs: Get urgent assessment for unexplained swelling of a single leg, sudden or severe swelling, a hot painful red area, fever or rapidly worsening symptoms. Swelling with breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, faintness or confusion needs emergency help. Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or throat with breathing or swallowing difficulty is also an emergency. During pregnancy, sudden increased swelling of the face, hands or feet, severe headache, visual symptoms or pain below the ribs needs immediate maternity advice because pre-eclampsia is possible. Do not drive yourself if seriously unwell.

sections.heading: Assessment and treatment target the cause
paragraphs: A clinician reviews medicines and medical history, examines the swelling and checks relevant body systems. Depending on the findings, blood or urine tests, ultrasound or other investigations may be appropriate. Treatment may involve a medicine review, care for an underlying disease or a plan for venous or lymphatic swelling. Diuretics are useful for some causes, not every swollen limb, and need individual prescribing and monitoring. Do not borrow water tablets or stop prescribed treatment yourself. Compression should be chosen after professional assessment of suitability and fit.

sections.heading: Everyday care needs an agreed plan
paragraphs: Once urgent causes have been excluded, gentle movement, avoiding long periods in one position, comfortable footwear and raising the legs may help suitable peripheral swelling. Wash, dry and care for the skin, reporting breaks or infection signs. Follow individual advice about salt, fluids and any weight monitoring; severe fluid restriction is not a general home remedy. Ask what changes require contact and when to review. If a familiar swelling suddenly changes character, seek reassessment rather than assuming the old plan still applies.

examples.title: A swollen calf after travel — hypothetical example
examples.text: After a long journey, a person develops new swelling and pain in a single calf. They arrange urgent assessment for a possible clot rather than assuming sitting is the whole explanation. Chest pain or breathlessness would require emergency help.

examples.title: Swelling during medicine treatment — hypothetical example
examples.text: Someone notices gradually tighter shoes after a medicine change. They tell the prescriber and bring a list of all treatments instead of stopping the new tablet or borrowing a diuretic. The clinician checks for medicine effects and other causes before changing the plan.

questions: What is the likely cause, and have urgent causes been considered?
Are compression, a medicine change or other treatments suitable for me?
What should I monitor, and which changes need urgent help or an earlier review?
